final_proof:
Let the mass distribution of the body be denoted by \(d\mu(x)\), so that \(M=\int_B d\mu(x)\). Let \(c\) be its centre of mass. Thus
\[
\int_B (x-c)\,d\mu(x)=0.
\]
Choose a unit vector \(u\) in the common direction of the two axes, and let \(P\) denote orthogonal projection onto the plane \(u^\perp\). Since \(A\) passes through \(c\), we have
\[
A=c+\mathbb R u.
\]
Because \(A'\) is parallel to \(A\), there is a unique vector \(a\in u^\perp\) such that
\[
A'=c+a+\mathbb R u.
\]
Indeed, \(a\) is the vector along the common perpendicular from \(A\) to \(A'\); consequently \(|a|=l\).

For \(x\in B\), put \(r(x)=P(x-c)\). Orthogonal projection onto \(u^\perp\) shows that the distances from \(x\) to the two axes are
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,A)=|r(x)|,\qquad
\operatorname{dist}(x,A')=|r(x)-a|.
\]
Therefore, by the definition of moment of inertia about an axis,
\[
I_0=\int_B |r(x)|^2\,d\mu(x)
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_B |r(x)-a|^2\,d\mu(x)\\
 &=\int_B |r(x)|^2\,d\mu(x)-2a\cdot\int_B r(x)\,d\mu(x)+|a|^2\int_B d\mu(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The middle term vanishes, because linearity of orthogonal projection and the centre-of-mass identity give
\[
\int_B r(x)\,d\mu(x)
=\int_B P(x-c)\,d\mu(x)
=P\left(\int_B(x-c)\,d\mu(x)\right)=0.
\]
Using also \(\int_Bd\mu=M\) and \(|a|=l\), we obtain
\[
I=I_0+M|a|^2=I_0+Ml^2,
\]
as claimed.
